LLM Output Detectability and Task Performance Can be Jointly Optimized Koshiro Saito1 Ryuto Koike1 Masahiro Kaneko2,1 Naoaki Okazaki1,3,4 1Institute of Science Tokyo 2MBZUAI 3National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology 4NII LLMC {koshiro.saito@nlp.,ryuto.koike@nlp.,okazaki@}comp.isct.ac.jp, masahiro.kaneko@mbzuai.ac.ae Abstract Detecting machine-generated text is essential for transparency and account- ability when deploying large language models (LLMs). Among detection approaches, watermarking is a statistically reliable method by design—it embeds detectable signals into LLM outputs by biasing their token dis- tributions. However, it has been reported that watermarked LLMs often perform worse on downstream tasks. We propose PUPPET, a framework that fine-tunes an LLM via reinforcement learning to generate text that is both more detectable and better performing on downstream tasks. We use two reward functions: a detector that outputs a machine-class likelihood and an evaluator that measures a task-specific metric. Experiments on long-form QA, summarization, and essay writing show that LLMs trained with PUPPET achieve high detectability competitive with watermarking methods while outperforming them on downstream tasks. The analysis shows that this optimization can be performed efficiently with only a few thousand samples in 1–2 GPU hours. Moreover, these gains are consistent across out-of-domain tasks, different LLM families, and model sizes, and are even robust to paraphrasing attacks. 1 Introduction LLMs now generate so fluent text that humans are almost unable to distinguish it from human-written text (Wang et al., 2025b; Clark et al., 2021; Jakesch et al., 2023). This raises urgent concerns about misuse, including academic fraud, spam, and automated disin- formation campaigns (Chen & Shu, 2024; Goldstein et al., 2023). Therefore, detecting machine-generated text is essential for transparency and accountability. From a LLM provider’s perspective, it is ideal for LLMs to be both highly detectable and strong on downstream tasks: high detectability supports accountability and misuse tracking, while strong task performance prevents users from exploring less detectable alternatives. Watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) is the de facto standard approach toward this goal— by biasing token distributions at generation time, it enables statistically reliable detection via a hypothesis test with a provably controlled false-positive rate. However, since this approach optimizes only detectability, the resulting output distribution deviates from what is optimal for downstream tasks, leading to task performance degradation (Ajith et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Fernandez et al., 2023). Directly optimizing the LLM for both detectability and task performance simultaneously would address this limitation. In

Experiments on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) across long-form QA, sum- marization, and essay generation show that PUPPET achieves comparable or superior detectability while consistently higher task performance, compared to five state-of-the-art watermarking methods: KGW (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023), SynthID (Dathathri et al., 2024), Unigram (Zhao et al., 2024), EXPGumbel (Aaronson, 2023), K-SemStamp (Hou et al., 2024b). For instance, on long-form QA, PUPPET improves both detectability and task performance by +3.8 and +2.6 points on average over those methods. Importantly, these gains generalize across out-of-domain tasks and different base LLMs and detectors, and remain robust even to paraphrasing attacks (Krishna et al., 2023)—a major challenge for watermarking methods. In addition, PUPPET is practically efficient, requiring only a few thousand samples and 1–2 GPU hours. For reproducibility, our PUPPET implementation is publicly available on GitHub1. 2 Proposed Method: PUPPET Figure 1 illustrates an overview of PUPPET. We build a preference dataset and apply DPO to the model π, jointly optimizing both detectability and task performance. We adopt DPO for its training stability compared with policy-gradient alternatives such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). We describe the details of the construction of the preference data in this section. First, we sample k responses tj (j ∈{1, . . . , k}) from the base model π for each input query q drawn from a query dataset Q (this dataset is task-specific): {t1, . . . , tk} ∼π(· | q). To select “chosen” and “rejected” responses from the candidates, we design two scores to assess the detectability and task performance of a generated text tj. The first is the detector score: the probability of the machine-generated class computed by a detector, SDet j = p(Machine | tj). The second is the evaluator score: a task-specific evaluation score assigned by an evaluator, SEval j = metric(tj), 1https://github.com/pakapaka333/PUPPET 2 Preprint. Under review. where metric(·) is a task-specific evaluation metric such as ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004) or LLM-as- a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023). The two scores are then combined into a final score for tj, Sj = α · z  SDet j  + (1 −α) · z  SEval j  , where z(·) denotes z-score normalization within the k samples to prevent either score from dominating due to differences in scale or variance, and α ∈[0, 1] is a hyperparameter controlling the relative emphasis between detectability and task performance. Setting α > 0.5 prioritizes detectability; and α < 0.5 prioritizes task performance. (2019)) from WaterBench (Tu et al., 2024), which is a standard benchmark for evaluating watermarking methods, and IELTS2 (essay generation), which provides a long-form, open- ended setting. For each dataset, we randomly sample 5,000 instances for training and 200 for evaluation without overlap. Base Model π We use Llama-3-8B-Instruct3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) as the primary base model for all main experiments. To assess the robustness to the choice of base model, we additionally evaluate on the Qwen3 model family (QwenTeam, 2025) in Section 5.2. Detector We use the OpenAI Detector (Solaiman et al., 2019) as the primary detector because it is widely used in prior work on machine-text detection (Nicks et al., 2024; Kushnareva et al., 2024). Additionally, we evaluate robustness to alternative classifiers in Section 5.2. We use AUROC as the evaluation metric for detection performance. Evaluator To investigate the effect of metric characteristics, we use ROUGE-L (reported as a percentage in [0, 100]), a lexical overlap metric, for ELI5 and Multi-News. For IELTS, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge score on a [0, 9] IELTS band scale to evaluate semantic quality. Training / Evaluation We fine-tune LLMs using DPO with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) for memory efficiency. We use a single fixed set of hyperparameters across all experiments for a controlled comparison, including k = 5 candidate responses (following Meng et al. (2024)) and α = 0.5. For evaluation, models generate responses equal in number to the human responses per sample (ELI5: 3, Multi-News: 1, IELTS: 1) to ensure fair metric computation. Baselines We compare PUPPET with five watermarking methods. Two are logit-based: KGW (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023), which biases green-list token logits conditioned on the preceding token, and Unigram (Zhao et al., 2024), which uses a fixed context-independent green list. Three are sampling-based: EXPGumbel (Aaronson, 2023), which resamples tokens via a seeded Gumbel distribution; SynthID (Dathathri et al., 2024), which selects tokens through a tournament over multiple random scores; and K-SemStamp (Hou et al., 2024b), which steers sentence-level generation toward a watermarked region in semantic embedding space. For additional details on training and evaluation settings, see Appendix A. 4 Results Table 1 presents the detection performance (AUROC) and task performance (ROUGE-L, Judge) of Llama-3 models trained with PUPPET across three benchmarks. We also visualize the token-level behavior of the responses using an ELI5 example in Figure 2. We draw two key observations. PUPPET improves both detection and task performance simultaneously. Compared to Vanilla, PUPPET improves AUROC by up to +12.3 points (IELTS: 87.0 →99.3), ROUGE- L by up to +2.9 points (ELI5: 22.9 →25.8), and LLM-as-a-Judge score by up to +0.42 points (IELTS: 6.77 →7.19). This confirms that PUPPET jointly optimizes both objectives, improving each relative to the Vanilla baseline. PUPPET outperforms watermarking baselines in task performance while matching their detectability. Llama-3 models trained with PUPPET achieve task performance levels that watermarked models cannot, with a gap of up to 6% on IELTS (SynthID: 6.76 vs. PUPPET: 7.19), while matching or surpassing them on detection. This provides intuitive evidence that DPO-based PUPPET leads the base LLM to acquire features that benefit both detectability and task performance, as intended. Note that the task performance degradation for watermarked models observed in prior work is not consistently reproduced in our experimental settings. We conjecture that this may be because recent LLMs can generate fluent text even under distributional constraints, though we do not conduct a dedicated analysis to substantiate this claim. Regardless, PUPPET’s contribution holds even in the absence of the reported degradation: PUPPET actively improves task performance to levels that watermarking methods cannot reach. 5 Analysis We conduct five analyses to further characterize PUPPET: (1) generalizability—whether PUPPET transfers to out-of-domain tasks, (2) robustness—whether PUPPET holds up across the different choices of base LLM, detector, and paraphrasing attacks, (3) efficiency—whether PUPPET can be applied with modest data resources, (4) reward ablation—whether both reward components are necessary for jointly optimizing both objectives, and (5) model attribution—whether PUPPET enables distinguishing its outputs from those of other models. 5.1 Generalizability to Out-of-Domain Tasks To assess whether PUPPET transfers beyond the tasks used during training, we evaluate the trained models on tasks not seen during training. Table 3 reports results for three Qwen3 variants (QwenTeam, 2025) and examines robustness to LLM choice along two sub-axes: model family and model size. Model family. Qwen3-8B is comparable in model size to Llama-3-8B-Instruct but belongs to a different model family, allowing us to isolate the effect of model family. PUPPET improves detection performance from 81.2 to 94.1 and task performance from 44.4 to 46.0 on average, demonstrating that its effectiveness generalizes beyond a single LLM family. Model size. We further evaluate Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B to assess PUPPET’s sensitivity to model size.4 PUPPET consistently improves both objectives across all model sizes. The detection gain is particularly large for Qwen3-14B (76.0 →97.4), where the stronger base model is intrinsically harder to detect, yet PUPPET still closes most of the gap. On the task side, PUPPET further improves each Vanilla baseline, regardless of size, demonstrating that PUPPET complements rather than undermines the capabilities of larger models. These results confirm that PUPPET’s effectiveness is not contingent on any particular model family or model size. We therefore examine PUPPET’s practicality along both dimensions. Figure 4 plots AUROC and task performance as a function of the number of training samples seen for Llama-3 across all three benchmarks. Across all benchmarks, both detectability and task performance rise sharply within the first few thousand samples and plateau near the level achieved with the full training set. For example, on ELI5, both performances converge within 1k–2k samples, with AUROC already reaching 100.0 at 1k samples. This handful of DPO pairs represents a remarkably small budget compared to large-scale DPO-based alignment pipelines such as OLMo3 (TeamOlmo, 2025), which train on 150K–200K pairs. Regarding compute, each training run completes in approximately 1–2 hours on a single NVIDIA A6000 (48GB) GPU. These results confirm that PUPPET is both data-efficient and computationally lightweight. The same trend holds for Qwen3 (Appendix E). 5.4 Reward Composition Ablation PUPPET uses a composite reward comprising a detector score (SDet) and an evaluator score (SEval). Optimizing detectability alone (SDet only) achieves large AUROC gains over Vanilla (up to +12.9 points) but degrades task performance (up to −1.5 ROUGE-L and −0.3 Judge). Con- versely, optimizing task performance alone (SEval only) yields meaningful improvements in it (up to +3.1 ROUGE-L and +0.8 Judge) but provides no reliable detection gain. PUPPET jointly optimizes both objectives and recovers 95.3–100% of the SDet-only detection gain while simultaneously improving task performance over Vanilla. These results confirm that both reward components are necessary: neither alone achieves strong performance across both objectives. Moreover, α provides a practical knob: higher values favor detectability, while lower values favor task performance. Detectors A standard approach involves training supervised classifiers on labeled datasets of human-written and machine-generated text. RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) is widely used as the base model (Solaiman et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024b; Tulchinskii et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024), and the RoBERTa-based OpenAI Detector (Solaiman et al., 2019) is widely used as a benchmark in prior work (Nicks et al., 2024; Kushnareva et al., 2024). A complementary, training-free paradigm exploits statistical properties of the genera- tion process. DetectGPT (Mitchell et al., 2023) exploits the observation that machine- generated text lies near local maxima of a model’s log-probability surface, so perturbations lower its log-probability, whereas human-written text does not exhibit this behavior. Fast- DetectGPT (Bao et al., 2024) achieves comparable accuracy at substantially lower cost by replacing perturbation-based estimation with conditional probability curvature sampling. Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024) achieves strong zero-shot detection by computing the ratio of cross-perplexity and perplexity between two related models. Watermarking Watermarking methods embed detectable signals into LLM-generated text and can be grouped into logit-based and sampling-based approaches. Logit-based methods bias the token output distribution at generation time. KGW (Kirchen- bauer et al., 2023) partitions the vocabulary into green and red lists conditioned on the preceding token, and increases the logits of green-list tokens by a fixed δ. Unigram (Zhao et al., 2024) simplifies this by using a fixed, context-independent green list, thereby making it more robust to token-substitution attacks. Both methods introduce systematic distortions into the output distribution, which has been shown to degrade task performance (Ajith et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Fernandez et al., 2023). Sampling-based methods, in contrast, intervene at the token selection stage without directly modifying logits. EXPGumbel (Aaronson, 2023) resamples tokens via a seeded Gumbel distribution, and SynthID (Dathathri et al., 2024) selects tokens through a tournament procedure over multiple random scores. K-SemStamp (Hou et al., 2024b) is a clustering- based extension of SemStamp (Hou et al., 2024a), which steers sentence-level generation toward watermarked regions in semantic embedding space. These methods are generally less disruptive to the output distribution than logit-based approaches, but task performance degradation can still be observed (Wang et al., 2025a). 9 Preprint. By jointly optimizing detectability and task performance, PUPPET matches watermarking methods in detection while surpassing them on downstream tasks—a combination that prior methods, which optimize only one objective at a time, cannot achieve. These gains generalize to out-of- domain tasks and prove robust to the choice of base LLM, detector, and paraphrasing attacks, all within moderate data and computational resources. Our exploratory analysis further suggests that PUPPET opens the door to model attribution. Two directions remain for future work: deeper mechanistic explanations of the acquired detect-relevant features, and systematic hyperparameter tuning—including the relative weighting of the two rewards—which may yield further gains. We hope this work encour- ages research into jointly optimizing LLMs across multiple accountability objectives, thereby contributing to more transparent deployment of language models. Ethics Statements Detection approaches, including PUPPET and watermarking, are still in the research stage. Therefore, it is essential to use these techniques with utmost caution under high-stakes set- tings where false positives (incorrectly identifying human-written text as machine-generated text) may cause significant harm.
